t.1.51.1: Though a boy, he speaks words like an elder; he is no boy, he is an elder in my view. I wish to grant him a boon; so give me your consent to it, O brahmins, all of you assembled together.
t.1.51.3: As the boon-granting king was about to say to the brahmin, "Choose a boon," the hotṛ priest, his inner self not greatly pleased, then spoke these words: "Takṣaka has not yet come to this rite."
t.1.51.2: A brahmin, even a boy, is rightly to be honored here by kings, whether he is unlearned or learned. This one deserves to receive all his wishes from you today, provided that Takṣaka comes to us quickly.
t.1.51.4: So that this rite of mine may be brought to completion, and so that Takṣaka may come to us swiftly, let all of you strive to the utmost of your power, for he is my enemy.
t.1.51.5: As the śāstras have told us, and as the fire declares, O king, Takṣaka, tormented by fear, is in the abode of Indra.
t.1.51.6: Just as the great-souled, red-eyed sūta, learned in the Purāṇas, had made known beforehand, so he, being questioned at that time, said to the king: “As the brahmins declare, so is this, O god among men.”
t.1.51.8: Hearing this, the consecrated king sat in anguish, urging on the Hotṛ at the time of the rite; and the Hotṛ, intent, made the offering with mantras, and then Indra himself came.
t.1.51.7: Having consulted the ancient lore, I therefore tell you, O king, that a boon was granted to him by Indra: “Dwell here near me, well protected, and the fire will not burn you.”
t.1.51.10: Hidden in his upper garment, that serpent, agitated with fear, found no refuge at all. Then the king, enraged and desiring the end of Takṣaka, spoke again to those versed in mantras.
t.1.51.9: Having mounted his celestial chariot, the mighty one was praised on all sides by all the gods and followed by clouds, by Vidyādharas, and by hosts of Apsarases.
t.1.51.11: O Brahmins, if that serpent Takṣaka is in the abode of Indra, then cast him down into the fire together with Indra himself!
t.1.51.12: Here comes Takṣaka swiftly into your power, O king; his great roar is heard as he cries out terribly in fear.
t.1.51.13: Surely that serpent has been let go by the wielder of the thunderbolt; fallen from his lap, his body loosened by the spells, the lord of serpents is approaching, whirling through the sky, his senses lost, breathing out fierce breaths.
t.1.51.14: This rite of yours, O king of kings, O lord, is proceeding according to rule; but you should grant a boon to this foremost of brahmins.
t.1.51.15: O immeasurable one, to you, a learned one though a boy, I grant a boon befitting you. Choose whatever is dear to you and settled in your heart; I shall give it to you even if it ought not to be given.
t.1.51.16: When Takṣaka, lord of the nāgas, was about to fall into the fire, Āstīka then urged them on, saying, "This is the moment!"
t.1.51.17: If you grant me a boon, O Janamejaya, I choose this: let this sacrifice of yours cease, and let no more serpents fall here.
t.1.51.18: Thus addressed, O brahmin, the king Pārikṣita, not very glad at heart, then spoke these words of faith.
t.1.51.20: Gold, silver and cows I do not ask of you, O king. Let this sacrifice of yours cease, so that there may be well-being for our mother's family.
t.1.51.19: Gold, silver, cows, and whatever else you have in mind, O lord, that I would give you as a boon, O brahmin; but let my sacrifice not be stopped.
t.1.51.21: Sūta said: Thus addressed by Āstīka, King Pārikṣita then spoke these words again and again to Āstīka, the best of speakers.
t.1.51.23: Then all the assembly members there, learned in the Veda, spoke together to the king: "Let the brahmin receive his boon."
t.1.51.22: "Choose another boon, O most excellent among the best of the twice-born, and may good fortune be yours!" But he did not ask for any other boon, O delight of the Bhṛgus.
